scenes.heading: Cells and microscopes
scenes.sub: What's inside a cell, and how do we measure it?
scenes.say: Every living thing, from a gum tree to you, is made of cells. But cells are far too small to see with your eyes. So how do biologists study them? With a microscope.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A house with a brick fence, solar panels and a water tank
scenes.science: A plant cell with a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole
scenes.breaks: a fence has a gate, but the cell wall has no door; the membrane underneath controls entry. And root cells have no chloroplasts.
scenes.say: Picture a plant cell as a house. The cell wall is a brick fence giving support. Chloroplasts are solar panels that capture light for photosynthesis. The large vacuole is a water tank that keeps the house firm. Animal cells are more like a tent.

scenes.heading: Cell theory
points: All living things are made of one or more cells
The cell is the smallest unit of life
All cells come from cells that already existed
scenes.say: Cell theory has three parts. All living things are made of one or more cells. The cell is the smallest unit of life. And all cells come from cells that already existed, by cell division.

scenes.heading: Plant vs animal cells
scenes.say: Both cell types have a membrane, cytoplasm, a nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes. Plant cells add a cell wall, a large vacuole and, in green parts, chloroplasts. Careful: no chloroplasts doesn't prove it's an animal cell. Root and onion cells lack them. Look for a cell wall or a large vacuole instead.

scenes.heading: Total magnification
scenes.say: Total magnification equals the eyepiece power times the objective power. Multiply, don't add. A ten times eyepiece with a forty times objective gives four hundred times, not fifty.
scenes.caption: Total magnification equals the eyepiece power × the objective power. Multiply, don't add. A 10× eyepiece with a 40× objective gives 400×, not 50×.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: At 40× the field of view is 4.5 mm. What is it at 400×? About 6 onion cells fit across. How long is one cell?
scenes.say: Zoom in, see less. Going from forty to four hundred times makes things ten times bigger, so the field of view shrinks ten times, to zero point four five millimetres. That's four hundred and fifty micrometres. Six cells fit across, so one cell is seventy-five micrometres.
scenes.caption: Zoom in, see less. Going from 40× to 400× makes things 10 times bigger, so the field of view shrinks 10 times, to 0.45 mm. That's 450 µm. 6 cells fit across, so one cell is 75 µm.

scenes.heading: Start low, go slow
steps: Start on the lowest power objective
Move the specimen to the centre
Switch up and use only fine focus
scenes.say: Good microscope technique: start on the lowest power objective and focus with the coarse knob. Move the specimen to the centre. Then switch to a higher objective and use only the fine focus knob, so you don't crack the slide.

points: All cells come from existing cells
Cell size = field of view ÷ cells across
scenes.say: Quick recap. All cells come from existing cells. Plant cells add a wall, a vacuole and chloroplasts. Multiply the lens powers. Zoom in, see less. Now try the practice questions!
